success_patterns: Definition-style clues ('sickle-shaped weapon of the Australian Aborigines', 'the sound a small object makes dropping into water') were solved by finding the dictionary or encyclopedia page whose text paraphrases the clue. The answer was that page's headword (Boomerang, plop), given bare without 'sound' or 'weapon'.

A clue naming two examples ('Vermont & Tillamook are American varieties of this cheese') was solved by finding the passage that lists both together ('Cheddars, as does Vermont and Tillamook'). The answer was the shared generic head noun (Cheddar), in the singular.

Where the verbatim clue appeared in passages but the answer was cut off (Bluebeard, Geppetto), the agent took it from other passages that restated the clue's descriptors next to a named entity (tags: 'bluebeard'; 'Geppetto is a poor, lonely wood carver'). It did not answer 'not answerable'.

A clue with an explicit '___' blank ('House Committee on ___ & Infrastructure') was solved by taking the word that fills the same slot in the repeated passage phrase ('Transportation and Infrastructure Committee').
Archive hits (StudyStack all-caps runs, local-word glosses like 'locally referred to as lambi') were copied in their short form, e.g. 'Sherbet', 'Conch'.

patch.reasoning: Several wins came from reading the passages in structured ways the skill does not yet spell out: (1) taking the headword of the dictionary page that paraphrases a definition clue, (2) finding the passage that lists both example anchors and answering the shared generic noun, (3) completing an archive hit whose answer is truncated from nearby passages that restate the clue's descriptors. These are broadly reusable. Each edit is short and fits an existing section, to avoid bloating the skill.

edits.target: and answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - Definition-style clues ('Sickle-shaped weapon of the Australian Aborigines', 'the sound a small object makes dropping into water, sometimes without a splash') have no 'this' pointer. Find the dictionary or encyclopedia page whose text paraphrases the clue ('the characteristic sound made by an object dropping into water without a splash'). The headword in its title ('Plop - definition of plop', 'Boomerang - Wikipedia') is the answer. Give that bare headword, without the category words the clue supplies ('sound', 'weapon'). A headword that recurs across several page titles beats a one-off word from a single passage.

edits.target: - 'X needs A & one of these' / 'A, B and one of these': the clue already gives some members of a set. Find the passage listing the full set ('a subject and a predicate') and answer with the missing member ('subject'), never one already named in the clue.
edits.content: - 'X & Y are varieties / examples / types of this <noun>' ('Vermont & Tillamook are American varieties of this cheese'): X and Y are anchors, never the answer. Find the passage that names both together ('England supplies many fine Cheddars, as does Vermont and Tillamook') and answer with the shared generic noun in the singular ('Cheddar'). Use the shared noun, not one of the named items or a branded product.

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - When the clue appears verbatim only in page titles or snippets that stop before any answer, do not give up. Read the other passages for lines that restate the clue's descriptors next to a named entity ('Geppetto is a poor, lonely wood carver'; tags such as 'edna st vincent millay, bluebeard'). Combine that with your own knowledge and answer with that entity. An explicit '___' blank in the clue works like a slot: take the word that fills the same position in the phrase the passages repeat ('Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure' -> 'Transportation').
